Nepalese authorities have banned Priyagold biscuits, manufactured by India's Surya Food and Agro Ltd, due to sub-standard quality and serious food safety violations, following action by India's FSSAI.

IMAGE: Kindly note that this image has been posted for representational purposes only. Photograph: Courtesy Priyagold on X

Key Points Nepalese authorities have banned the import, sales, and distribution of Priyagold biscuits from India.

The ban was issued on Monday by Nepal's Food Technology and Quality Control Department, citing the product as sub-standard.

India's FSSAI initiated legal proceedings against Surya Food and Agro Ltd for using cattle feed bran and other serious food safety violations.

FSSAI also suspended the licence of Surya Food and Agro after observing serious hygiene deficiencies during an inspection.

Nepal's department urged traders and consumers to halt sales and recall existing stocks from the market.

Nepalese authorities have banned import, sales and distribution of Priyagold biscuits manufactured by Surya Food and Agro Ltd in India.

Nepal's Ban on Priyagold Biscuits

Issuing a notice on Monday, the food technology and quality control department of Nepal imposed restrictions on import, sales, and distribution of Priya Gold biscuits manufactured by India's Surya Food and Agro Ltd, describing the product as sub-standard.

India's food regulator FSSAI has initiated legal proceedings for prosecution against Surya Food & Agro for using cattle feed bran in manufacturing of Priyagold biscuits and for other serious violations.

While conducting an inspection of Surya Food and Agro, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) observed serious food safety and hygiene deficiencies, the authority said.

FSSAI Action and Consumer Safety

The FTQCD banned the import and sale of Priyagold biscuits on the basis of the notice published by FSSAI, which has also suspended the licence of Surya Food and Agro.

The decision to ban Priyagold biscuit was taken after virtually conducting an emergency meeting at the initiative of director general of the department Sanjeev Kumar Karna, taking into consideration the human health security and protection of the consumer's welfare, the notice stated.

The department has urged all bodies concerned, traders and consumers not import the biscuit hereafter and halt its sales and distribution.

The department has also asked the authorised importer and food traders to immediately recall the products from the market, if there are stocks.

title: Nepal: Still no justice for protesters one year on as journalists and critics continue to be targeted - Civicus Monitor
description: Nepal: Still no justice for protesters one year on as journalists and critics continue to be targeted  Civicus Monitor
publisher.title: Civicus Monitor
full_article:
Family members of those killed hold a vigil at a memorial ceremony marking the first anniversary of the protests in Kathmandu (Photo Credit: Sanjit Pariyar/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

The state of civic space in Nepal is rated as ‘obstructed’ by the CIVICUS Monitor. Documented violations of fundamental freedoms include the targeting of journalists, including through harassment, attacks and criminalisation, and arbitrary arrests and the use of excessive force with impunity during protests. At least 1,400 people were killed, including 84 children, and nearly 5,300 people are still missing, after a mountain of glacial ice and rock collapsed into the Bhotekoshi, Upper Trishuli and Narayani-Gandak rivers on 26th August 2026, unleashing a massive flood. It affected communities and critical infrastructure across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, Chitwan and surrounding areas. The flood swept through riverside settlements, damaging homes, roads, bridges, hydropower facilities and other essential infrastructure. Nearly two months later, communities are still struggling to rebuild their lives. In recent months, there has been lack of accountability for the 2025 protests. Journalists continue to be targeted for their reporting, with arrests, raids, harassment and attacks. Police arrested a political analyst for his social media comments and detained a protester at a government event. A comedian reported threats over his political satire, while a centralised “one-door” aid system creates obstacles for civil society response to floods. Peaceful Assembly Lack of accountability for 2025 protests One year on from the mass protests in September 2025 that brought a change of government but led to 76 deaths and hundred of injuries, there has been a lack of accountability. The inquiry commission led by former Supreme Court justice Gauri Bahadur Karki recommended criminal prosecution, concluding that citizens had died due to negligence by those in positions of political leadership. While Home Minister Sudan Gurung and others directed the arrest of Oli and Lekhak the day after Shah took the oath of office. Although Oli and Lekhak were released about two weeks after their arrests, the criminal investigation against them remains pending. In March 2026, police arrested former Prime Minister KP Oli and former Home Affairs Minister Ramesh Lekhak for their alleged involvement in the deadly crackdown on the protesters. Both men were released in April 2026 and have not been formally charged. However, police have not proceeded with questioning other people linked to the incident, collecting additional evidence or examining documents. Although the Karki commission and the National Human Rights Commission investigated the incident, detailed documents identifying those involved in the use of force and analysing their accountability are not publicly available. Further, the recommendations have yet to be implemented. At a memorial marking the first anniversary of the protests, speakers accused the government of failing to honour commitments made to injured protesters and the families of those killed. They demanded action against those responsible for the shootings, proper treatment for the injured, and the release of young protesters who remain in jail for their involvement in the movement. Committee submits report on withdrawal of criminal cases against protesters A committee formed to study the withdrawal of criminal cases filed against Gen Z protesters completed its study and submitted a report to Home Minister Sudhan Gurung on 1st October 2026. According to some reports, there are about 900 still in detention. Some individuals involved in the protest are in pre-trial detention. The committee has suggested that approximately 100 cases with insufficient evidence, weak evidence, or unspecified compensation amounts can be withdrawn. Expression Journalist arrested and equipment seized by police

Kishor Shrestha, editor-in-chief of the weekly newspaper Jana Astha, was taken to the Cyber Bureau of Nepal Police on Friday for discussion following a complaint filed against him. https://t.co/x2MyOTsrjo — Onlinekhabar English (@OnlineKhabar_En) October 17, 2026

In August 2026, Kathmandu police raided the Jana Aastha Weekly newsroom after editor-in-chief Kishor Shrestha was arrested over a privacy complaint. Police arrested journalist Kishor Shrestha on 12th August 2026 in Lalitpur, after a complaint alleged a photograph and news report published by Jana Aastha Weekly violated Nepal’s Privacy Act, 2018. The photograph pictured lawmaker Amarkant Chaudhary with the complainant and was reportedly sourced from her public Facebook page. Police subsequently raided Shrestha’s home and the Jana Aastha office, seizing communication devices, CPUs and computers as evidence. Shrestha is known for his investigative journalism, with Jana Aastha having a reputation for independent and critical reporting. He serves as vice president of the World Press Council and was Press Council Nepal’s former chairperson. In a statement on his release, the journalist said he was not allowed to meet with his lawyer during his detention. He was released on bail, with the investigation ongoing, after the Supreme Court ruled the investigation no longer warranted continued custody. Supreme Court justices also ordered news content complaints be managed through Nepal’s Press Council, which has an existing protocol to address grievances while ensuring press freedom is upheld. The Federation of Nepali Journalists (FNJ) deplored “the government’s abuse of state mechanisms to bypass the Press Council and arrest senior journalist Kishor Shrestha. The police raids on his home and Jana Aastha offices are an attack on democratic values and global norms of a free press.” Media Action Nepal said it was gravely concerned about the police action. They added: “Entering a newsroom and seizing technical equipment without following established procedures raises serious concerns regarding democratic norms, press freedom, and constitutional safeguards.” On 16th October 2026, Kishor Shrestha was taken to the Cyber Bureau of the police following a complaint filed against him by Rastriya Swatantra Party central committee member Himesh Pant. The dispute stems from a Jana Aastha report alleging that Pant’s family had grabbed land belonging to Tilak Prasad Bidari of Thakre Rural Municipality-10 in Dhading. Journalists targeted for their reporting Since August 2026, journalists have continued to be targeted for their reporting, including being barred, harassed and attacked. On 11th July 2026, it was reported by Freedom Forum that journalists were barred from reporting on the situation of displaced people at government holding centres in Kathmandu, Bagmati Province. They had been displaced following the demolition of riverside settlements for alleged encroachment on government land. Several journalists shared incidents of intimidation and obstruction during their reporting. In August 2026, Editor of Nepalkarma.com, Sushil Khadka, was harassed over his reporting in Surkhet, Karnali Province. He had covered a news story about alleged violence against women that was published on the portal on 29th July. However, he was later threatened and accused of publishing false information. On 25th September 2026, journalists were verbally abused and manhandled while covering an event in Morang, Koshi Province. Makalu Television reporter Dilip Agrawal told Freedom Forum that he and two colleagues were covering a municipal assembly. While taking a statement from municipal chief Bikash Siwakoti, he pushed Agrawal and verbally abused him. Municipal Chief Siwakoti also manhandled Chandan Paswan, a reporter for Koshi Awaj online. Police arrest political analyst for his social media comments

Bharat Mani Dahal arrested on cybercrime charges https://t.co/F4msL63DfP — Setopati (@setopati) September 20, 2026

Political analyst Bharat Dahal was arrested by police in Belbari, Morang on 20th September 2026 and brought to Kathmandu for investigation under Section 47 of the Electronic Transactions Act. Dahal, who is also chair of the Trimool Nepal Party, had made political comments and gave interviews in which he alleged that the Gen Z movement and some of its leaders had been influenced or mobilised by foreign powers. Dahal had cited material published by The Grayzone while making claims about the Gen Z protests and alleged external influence. He was arrested after such content circulated on social media. On 21st September 2026 the Kathmandu District Court had granted police a three-day remand to investigate Dahal. Freedom Forum said it was “concerned over the arrest and detention of Dahal. Arresting an individual solely for sharing a report on social media is a sheer violation of freedom of expression and opinion. Resorting to cybercrime offence merely for sharing a news report and expressing political views on social media risks misuse of the Electronic Transactions Act (ETA) and has a chilling effect on freedom of expression.” On 24th September 2026, the Supreme Court observed that Dahal’s recent statements amounted to an exercise of his freedom of thought and expression and ordered that he be released from custody. The court said the investigation file did not show sufficient grounds for keeping Dahal in custody. The Supreme Court therefore said that if further investigation was required, it could be conducted while Dahal remained outside custody. title: Nepal secure crucial win over Oman in bid to retain ODI status - OnlineKhabar English News
description: Nepal secure crucial win over Oman in bid to retain ODI status  OnlineKhabar English News
publisher.title: OnlineKhabar English News
full_article:
Kathmandu, October 19

Nepal made a remarkable comeback with the ball to defeat Oman by 10 runs in their final ICC Cricket World Cup League 2 match on Monday, securing sixth place in the standings.

In the match played at Al Amerat Ground, Oman, chasing a target of 281, managed 270 for six in their 50 overs.

Jatinder Singh top-scored for Oman with 89 runs, while Hammad Mirza contributed 87. The pair put Oman in a strong position after adding 158 runs for the second wicket, having lost their first wicket for 32.

After dismissing the partnership at 190, Nepal struck again just 13 runs later. Oman subsequently slipped to 203 for three and 206 for four before captain Vinayak Shukla was dismissed at 224 for five. Sanju Sajiv was then run out, leaving Oman at 232 for six.

Hasnain Shah kept Oman in contention with an unbeaten 40 off 23 balls, hitting several boundaries towards the end. However, he could not take his side over the line.

Needing 23 runs from the final over, Oman faced Nepal’s Dipendra Singh Airee. Hasnain scored two runs off the first ball before hitting two consecutive fours, leaving Oman needing 13 from three balls. After taking two more runs, Oman needed 11 off the final two deliveries. Airee bowled a dot ball before Hasnain failed to score off the last ball, sealing Nepal’s victory.

Three half-centuries lift Nepal to 280

Earlier, Nepal won the toss and elected to bat, posting 280 runs before being bowled out in 50 overs.

Dev Khanal, Rohit Paudel and Dipendra Singh Airee scored half-centuries to lead Nepal’s innings.

Paudel scored 80 off 81 balls, hitting two fours and two sixes. Airee made 69 off 62 deliveries, including three fours and four sixes, while opening batter Khanal contributed 57 off 65 balls, with four fours and a six.

Nepal were struggling at 99 for three when Paudel and Airee combined for a 139-run partnership to rebuild the innings.

However, Nepal failed to finish strongly, losing their remaining wickets after reaching 238 for three. Basir Ahmed provided a late boost with 17 runs off just seven balls, including two fours and a six.

For Oman, Shah Faisal claimed five wickets for 57 runs in eight overs. Jay Odedra took three wickets, while Samay Shreevastav claimed two.

Nepal return to sixth place

The victory was crucial for Nepal, who needed to win to finish among the top six teams in the World Cup League 2 standings.

Nepal had won their opening two matches against Canada and Oman before losing to Canada on Saturday.

Following that defeat, Canada climbed to sixth place with 29 points from 36 matches, pushing Nepal down to seventh with 28 points from 35 matches.

Monday’s win lifted Nepal back to sixth place, giving them 30 points from 36 matches.

Finishing in the top six is significant because those teams have a strong chance of retaining their One Day International status. Nepal’s victory over Oman therefore proved decisive in its bid to secure a top-six finish in the League 2 campaign.

title: Habitat for Humanity highlights Nepal's growing housing crisis - KEYE
description: Habitat for Humanity highlights Nepal's growing housing crisis  KEYE
publisher.title: KEYE
full_article:
A safe place to call home is something every family deserves. But for communities across Nepal, finding secure and affordable housing has become an increasingly difficult challenge, made even more urgent by devastating flash floods and extreme weather.

New global research from Habitat for Humanity reveals the enormous pressure families in Nepal were already facing before the recent disaster.

Eliza Sthapit, National Director of Habitat for Humanity Nepal, joined We Are Austin to discuss the findings, the challenges facing families and why building stronger, more resilient homes is critical for the future.

Watch the full video above to learn more about Habitat for Humanity's work in Nepal!

Housing is a major source of stress for families

According to Habitat for Humanity's global research, 68% of people surveyed in Nepal identified housing as one of the biggest sources of stress in their lives.

That's nearly double the 35% reported across the countries surveyed.

The findings highlight how deeply housing concerns affect families, even before natural disasters place additional pressure on communities.

For many households, the struggle to find safe, stable housing is about much more than having a roof overhead. It can affect financial security, health and a family's ability to plan for the future.

Extreme weather adds to an existing crisis

Recent flash floods across Nepal have brought renewed attention to the importance of safe housing and disaster preparedness.

For families already facing housing insecurity, severe weather can create additional challenges, including damage to homes, displacement and the difficult process of rebuilding.

As communities work toward recovery, Habitat for Humanity is emphasizing the need for housing solutions that address both immediate needs and future risks.

What is resilient housing?

Building a home is one thing. Building a home that can better withstand future disasters is another.

Resilient housing refers to homes designed, constructed or improved to better withstand environmental hazards, including flooding, severe storms and other climate-related threats.

The goal is not simply to rebuild after a disaster, but to help families and communities become better prepared for the next one.

For Nepal, where challenging terrain and extreme weather can increase risks, resilient housing is an important part of long-term community stability.

A global challenge with local impact

While Nepal faces its own unique housing challenges, Habitat for Humanity's research highlights a larger issue affecting families around the world.

Housing affordability, safety and stability are concerns that extend across borders, including here in the United States.

By examining how families experience housing stress in different countries, the research helps bring greater attention to the human impact of the global housing crisis.

How you can help

Habitat for Humanity continues working with communities around the world to expand access to safe, affordable housing and support long-term resilience.

Through community partnerships, housing initiatives and disaster recovery efforts, the organization aims to help more families build a stable foundation for the future.

To explore the research, learn more about Habitat for Humanity's work or find ways to get involved, visit Habitat.org.

title: China cites non-existent Tibetan refugee threats to refuse reopening Nepal border trade post - Tibetan Review
description: China cites non-existent Tibetan refugee threats to refuse reopening Nepal border trade post  Tibetan Review
publisher.title: Tibetan Review
full_article:
(TibetanReview.net, Oct19’26) – The Tatopani crossing in Sindhupalchok is the most viable route for Nepal to conduct border trade with China through Tibet. However, despite intensified diplomatic efforts from Kathmandu, China remains unwilling to reopen it for regular border exchanges due mainly to its security concerns related to unsubstantiated allegations of Tibetan refugee movements and activities.

The border point has been opened only temporarily, for just three days, to facilitate the import of goods for the Dashain festival, reported english.nepalnews.com Oct 18. The festival is Nepal’s longest, grandest, and most important, and lasts 15 days and began on Oct 11 this year. It is celebrated to honour Goddess Durga and her victory over the demon Mahishasura.

Nepal intensified its diplomatic efforts to reopen the Tatopani border crossing with China after floods and landslides disrupted alternative trade routes, but Beijing has yet to commit to restoring regular operations, citing security concerns, logistical difficulties and recurring landslides, reported kathmandupost.com Oct 17.

The report cited Nepali officials familiar with border security as saying Chinese concerns about Tibetan refugees entering Nepal and possible anti-China activities along the frontier had also complicated efforts to resume trade through the Tatopani crossing.

Reopening the Tatopani crossing has become more urgent since the Aug 26 Bhotekoshi flood closed the Rasuwa­gadhi border point, Nepal’s major trade route with China through Tibet. But China is only offering assistance to restore Rasuwa­gadhi as the main trading point, although even this is bound to take a long time.

The Tatopani crossing in Sindhupalchok, Nepal.

The Korala border crossing in Mustang, another alternative, also remains disrupted by floods and landslides, leaving goods ordered by traders stranded ahead of Dashain, Nepal’s most widely celebrated festival and the biggest shopping season of the year, the report said.

At a meeting on Oct 14 with Nepal’s Industry, Commerce and Supplies Minister Deepak Kumar Sah, Chinese Ambassador Zhang Maoming indicated that Tatopani could be reopened for a short period to meet festival demand, but that its long-term operation would require a detailed assessment. The ambassador has mainly cited security challenges, while also referring to logistical problems and frequent landslides as additional complications.

Beijing’s wider concerns was stated to be its allegations of cross-border movement of Tibetan refugees along the Nepal-Tibet border.

The report noted that during the government led by the Nepal Communist Party, formed through the merger of the CPN-UML and the Maoists, the home ministry decided to stop deporting Tibetan refugees to India. It bears noting that this was a result of international pressure, especially from the United sates. It cited a former senior administrator who served as chief district officer in Sindhupalchok as saying Chinese officials continued to provide information about people crossing from Tibet, and Nepali authorities acted on some of those reports.

A former chief district officer in Sindhupalchok has recalled Chinese officials expressing concern over the alleged growing presence of followers of the Dalai Lama in border areas. However, investigations by Nepal Police and the National Investigation Department did not establish the scale of activity claimed by the Chinese side, the report noted.

“There may be people using the area as a transit point, but we did not find the kind of followers they described,” the former official has said, adding that subsequent administrative action had made such activity less likely.

Another former additional chief research director of the National Investigation Department has said the number of young Tibetans leaving their homes and coming to Nepal had declined as China had developed Tibet and sought to relocate settlements further inland, away from the border.

The report said that a few years ago, China had proposed forming a joint monitoring team with Nepal, comprising officials from the administration in Tibet and their counterparts in Sindhupalchok.

“The proposal was put forward as a way to coordinate responses to disasters and other issues, and it reached the home secretary through the relevant channel. The district security committee also endorsed it and forwarded it. But ultimately, the ministry didn’t approve it,” the report quoted the official as saying.

The report said that despite these concerns, officials and traders say the crossing’s economic importance warrants a fresh effort to reach an understanding with Beijing.

Tatopani was closed following the 2015 earthquake and reopened for limited cargo movement in May 2019. It was again closed during the Covid pandemic in 2020. Imports remained restricted largely to selected goods, while exports have struggled to resume meaningfully despite China permitting outbound trade in 2023. Before the earthquake, Nepal exported copper utensils, handicrafts, flour, noodles, eggs, vegetable ghee and medicinal herbs through the crossing, the report said.

The Araniko Highway, built in the 1960s, was stated to be Nepal’s principal road link with China through before the Rasuwa­gadhi-Kerung route opened in 2014. Repeated closures have since weakened Tatopani’s role, the report said.

title: Long Island families left with uncertainty after Nepal ends flood rescue - Newsday
description: Long Island families left with uncertainty after Nepal ends flood rescue  Newsday
publisher.title: Newsday
full_article:
Nearly two months after flash floods swept through the Nepal-China border region, Rajendra Karki, of Hicksville, is still holding onto hope his sister Krishna Kumari Shrestha, 62, is somewhere out there.

Though Nepalese officials told Karki's family his sister likely hadn’t survived the flood, he still was upset to hear search and rescue efforts have ceased.

"We hope they magically find our sister. ... I wish they’d continue searching for people. We don’t know if my sister died. We’re all hoping they’re alive," said Karki, 48, who told Newsday Krishna was at home with three relatives — Dhan Kumari Shrestha, 64; Deb Kumari Shrestha, 59; Kopila Shreatha, 36 — when the flood inundated the Himalayan region.

A September report from World Weather Attribution said the Aug. 26 disaster was caused by a rock-ice avalanche that evolved into a debris flood. The nonprofit found human-caused warming that melted glaciers and thawed frozen ground likely further destabilized an already vulnerable mountain slope.

Last week, the office of Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah announced it concluded search and rescue operations for victims of the floods, The Associated Press reported. The bodies of at least 1,455 people have been recovered, but 5,285 remain missing.

The president of the Long Island Nepalese Society, Sabitra Siwakoti, said the decision to halt the search and rescue effort has generated mixed emotions within her group. Some believe the Nepalese government did everything it could, while others wish search efforts would continue a bit longer.

"Even one body is a big deal for us. That’s a human being. But unfortunately, this disaster [came without] any warning," Siwakoti said. "Personally, I feel like they try their best. ... The Nepali government spent a lot of money and lots of resources to search for them as far as we know."

Siwakoti said many members of the group wanted to fly to Nepal to support their families but concluded that money was better spent contributing to the Nepalese government’s search efforts and financially supporting displaced relatives.

"I tried to go right away, but my parents said, ‘It’s too fresh, and even if you come here, you cannot do anything right now. You'd just be crying. That's what we're doing here,’ " said Karki, who watched from afar as his family priest cremated bodies made of kusha grass to represent his four missing relatives in a Hindu ceremony, called Pratika Antyeshti.

With recent developments, he hopes to return as soon as possible to help memorialize his sister, who was a retired school teacher.

Just days before the floods, Karki said his sister sent him a message wishing him blessings for the Hindu festival Rakhi, which celebrates the bond between brothers and sisters.

He hadn’t initially panicked after being unable to contact her after the disaster. But when her husband and two sons called days later, Karki knew something was wrong.

"They were crying and that’s when I knew the news. ... I could not believe that. It’s not possible. Her home is not close to the river. I said, ‘How could the flood go that high?’," he said.

Newsday also followed up with Aditi Patel, who said in September her mother, Tejal Vyomesh Patel, her mother-in-law, Amita Amin and family friend Jitendra Manubhai Patel had crossed the border into Tibet with a tour group at the time of the catastrophic floods. About 400 family members and friends of the tour group gathered in Queens on Sept. 27 for a prayer meeting.

Unanswered questions

Amita Amin, 67, of Roslyn Heights, left, and Tejal Vyomesh Patel, 64, of New Jersey, went missing after the deadly floods. Credit: Nepal Trekking Planner

Patel, 42, of Old Westbury, said she received death certificates for her mother and mother-in-law from the Nepalese government on Friday morning, which she obtained via email from the United States government.

"It was not easy seeing that in the email," Patel said. "It was kind of like this is the end of the road."

She did not receive one for their friend.

While the documents provide some closure, Patel said some questions are left unanswered. "Mentally, our closure would be knowing exactly where they were."

Patel and her father-in-law traveled to Nepal in September and met with the owner of the tour group company, whose own son-in-law and guide on the trip are missing. They also took a helicopter ride with the Nepalese army.

"You think you see it just like in videos and you think you know it, and then seeing it in person, it just hits you 20 times harder," Patel said. "There is no way anybody would have made it out alive if they were within that disaster zone."

Seeing the full scope of the disaster also gave them perspective on just how many people it affected, as the mudslides wiped out "countless other lives, houses, businesses," as well as entire families.

"It just seemed not so just personal to us anymore. It just seemed like such a big humanitarian crisis. ... There are thousands of other people like us," Patel said.

Patel said recent identifications of 9/11 victims gave her hope that someday, her loved ones' DNA could be confirmed through collection of samples.

But right now, Patel said the hardest thing about this is someday explaining it all to her children, who are too young to understand.

"They ask about them, they talk about them and it doesn't make it easier for us," Patel said. "This seems unfair that they have to be without both their grandmothers."
